es.term: Insuficiencia cardíaca con fracción de eyección reducida (ICFEr)
es.summary: Disfunción sistólica del ventrículo izquierdo que reduce la fracción de eyección (<40%). Provoca bajo gasto cardíaco y congestión sistémica.
key_points: Aumento de la presión de llenado y activación neurohormonal
Edema periférico y pulmonar son signos clásicos
Tratamiento combina diuréticos, IECA/ARA II, betabloqueadores y antagonistas de aldosterona

pathophysiology: Daño miocárdico disminuye contractilidad del ventrículo izquierdo.
Disminuye el volumen sistólico y la fracción de eyección (<40%).
Compensa con aumento de frecuencia cardíaca y activación del sistema renina‑angiotensina‑aldosterona.
Retención de sodio y agua genera sobrecarga de volumen y congestión pulmonar y sistémica.
risk_factors: Enfermedad arterial coronaria o infarto previo.
signs_symptoms: Disnea de esfuerzo que progresa a reposo.
Fatiga y disminución de la tolerancia al ejercicio.
diagnostics: Ecocardiograma: fracción de eyección <40% y dilatación ventricular.
Radiografía de tórax: cardiomegalia y edema intersticial.
Electrocardiograma: signos de hipertrofia o isquemia.
treatment: Inhibidores de la ECA (ej. enalapril) o ARA‑II (losartán).
Antagonistas de los receptores de aldosterona (espironolactona).
Diuréticos de asa (furosemida) para controlar la sobrecarga de volumen.
Terapia de resincronización cardíaca o desfibrilador en casos seleccionados.
complications: Insuficiencia renal por bajo flujo renal.
nursing_care: Evaluar signos vitales cada 4 h; prestar atención a PA, FC y saturación O₂.
Monitorear peso diario; registrar aumento >2 kg/48 h como alerta de retención.
Posicionar al paciente semi‑sentado (30‑45°) para mejorar la ventilación.
Administrar diuréticos según orden y observar salida de orina.
Educación sobre restricción de sodio (<2 g/día) y adherencia al tratamiento.
patient_teaching: Reconocer signos de empeoramiento: disnea creciente, edema, aumento de peso.
Importancia de la dieta baja en sodio y control de líquidos.
Tomar los medicamentos exactamente como se indican, sin omitir dosis.
Registrar peso diario y reportar cambios al profesional de salud.
Mantener actividad física moderada según tolerancia y guía médica.

outcomes: Gasto cardíaco: aumento a >4 L/min en 48 h
Perfusión tisular periférica: piel cálida y sin cianosis en 72 h

interventions.action: Evaluar FC, PA y saturación O₂ cada 4 h
Registrar peso diario y comparar con la línea base
Administrar diurético de asa según prescripción y monitorear diuresis
interventions.rationale: Reducir sobrecarga de volumen y mejorar el gasto

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre restricción de sodio y adherencia al tratamiento
interventions.rationale: Disminuir la activación neurohormonal y mejorar la función cardíaca

interventions.action: Colaborar con el médico para ajustar IECA y betabloqueador según respuesta
interventions.rationale: Optimizar la terapia que aumenta el gasto cardíaco

outcomes: Equilibrio electrolítico: K⁺ 3.5‑5.0 mEq/L en 72 h

interventions.action: Obtener y registrar electrolitos séricos cada 24 h mientras esté en diuréticos
Evaluar signos de hipocalemia (debilidad muscular, arritmias)
Administrar suplemento de potasio oral o IV según indicación
interventions.rationale: Mantener K⁺ dentro del rango terapéutico

interventions.action: Instruir al paciente sobre alimentos ricos en potasio (plátano, papas)
Monitorear ingesta y salida de líquidos para evitar hipovolemia
interventions.rationale: Preservar la perfusión renal y el equilibrio de Na⁺

en.term: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)
en.summary: Systolic dysfunction of the left ventricle that reduces ejection fraction (<40%). Causes low cardiac output and systemic congestion.
key_points: Increased filling pressure and neurohormonal activation
Peripheral and pulmonary edema are classic signs
Treatment combines diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta‑blockers, and aldosterone antagonists

pathophysiology: Myocardial damage decreases left ventricular contractility.
Decreases stroke volume and ejection fraction (<40%).
Compensates with increased heart rate and activation of the renin‑angiotensin‑aldosterone system.
Sodium and water retention causes volume overload and pulmonary and systemic congestion.
risk_factors: Coronary artery disease or prior myocardial infarction.
diagnostics: Echocardiogram: ejection fraction <40% and ventricular dilation.
Chest X‑ray: cardiomegaly and interstitial edema.
Electrocardiogram: signs of hypertrophy or ischemia.
treatment: Loop diuretics (furosemide) to control volume overload.
Cardiac resynchronization therapy or implantable defibrillator in selected cases.
complications: Renal failure from low renal perfusion.
nursing_care: Assess vital signs every 4 h; monitor BP, HR, and O₂ saturation.
Monitor daily weight; record >2 kg/48 h as a retention alert.
Position patient semi‑upright (30‑45°) to improve ventilation.
Administer diuretics as ordered and observe urine output.
Educate on sodium restriction (<2 g/day) and medication adherence.
patient_teaching: Recognize worsening signs: increasing dyspnea, edema, weight gain.
Importance of low‑sodium diet and fluid control.
Take medications exactly as prescribed, do not miss doses.
Record daily weight and report changes to the health professional.
Maintain moderate physical activity as tolerated and per medical guidance.

outcomes: Cardiac output: increase to >4 L/min in 48 h
Peripheral tissue perfusion: warm skin without cyanosis in 72 h

interventions.action: Assess HR, BP, and O₂ saturation every 4 h
Record daily weight and compare to baseline
Administer loop diuretic per prescription and monitor diuresis
interventions.rationale: Reduce volume overload and improve output

interventions.action: Educate patient on sodium restriction and medication adherence
interventions.rationale: Decrease neurohormonal activation and improve cardiac function

interventions.action: Collaborate with physician to adjust ACE inhibitor and beta‑blocker per response
interventions.rationale: Optimize therapy that increases cardiac output

outcomes: Electrolyte balance: K⁺ 3.5‑5.0 mEq/L in 72 h

interventions.action: Obtain and record serum electrolytes every 24 h while on diuretics
Assess signs of hypokalemia (muscle weakness, arrhythmias)
Administer oral or IV potassium supplement as indicated
Instruct patient on potassium‑rich foods (banana, potatoes)
Monitor fluid intake and output to avoid hypovolemia
interventions.rationale: Preserve renal perfusion and Na⁺ balance

summary.0.quote: Conversely, patients with ejection fractions less than 40 percent have a higher risk for developing serious dysrhythmias.

key_points.0.quote: Type of Heart Failure Criteria Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) Left ventricular ejection fraction ≤40%

key_points.2.quote: The classic presentation of HF includes lower extremity edema, weight gain, cough, sputum production, and alterations in hemodynamics.

key_points.3.quote: Pharmacological agents utilized in the treatment of HF include beta-blockers, diuretics, ACE inhibitor s/ARBs, and nitrates.

sections.pathophysiology.3.quote: A sodium-restricted diet (less than 2000 mg of sodium per day) may help maintain euvolemia (normal blood volume) and prevent clients from becoming overloaded with fluid (which presents as pitting edema in the extremities, abdominal edema, and/or pulmonary edema).

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: There are multiple causes of HFrEF, including coronary artery disease and acute myocardial infarction (AMI).

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: Symptoms associated with heart failure include shortness of breath, edema, exercise intolerance, and fatigue.

sections.diagnostics.1.quote: Normal levels of BNP should be less than 100 pg/mL, and may increase slightly due to age, but assessing levels along with the clinical presentations assists the nurse to evaluate the patient’s response to treatment.

sections.diagnostics.2.quote: If the patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of HF, chest X-rays assist with identifying pulmonary edema or cardiomegaly , which means ventricular enlargement to accommodate excess fluid ( Figure 12.20 ).

sections.treatment.0.quote: Class Drug Dosing ACE inhibitor Lisinopril 2.5/5/10/20/40 mg per day Benazepril 10/20/40 mg per day Enalapril 2.5/5/10/20 mg per day Captopril 6.25-12.5 mg PO every 8 hours Angiotensin-receptor blocker Losartan 25/50/100 mg per day Valsartan 40/80/160/320 mg per day Irbesartan 150/300 mg per day Olmesartan 10/20/40 mg per day Table 12.3 Common ACE

sections.treatment.1.quote: Cardio-selective beta-blockers such as metoprolol work exclusively on the beta (1) sites in the heart, whereas carvedilol, a nonselective beta-blocker, works on both beta (1) and beta (2) sites.

sections.treatment.3.quote: Considered preload reducers, potent diuretics such as furosemide work on the loop of Henle and increase fluid excretion.

sections.complications.0.quote: If the patient is experiencing an acute exacerbation of HF, chest X-rays assist with identifying pulmonary edema or cardiomegaly , which means ventricular enlargement to accommodate excess fluid ( Figure 12.20 ).

sections.nursing_care.1.quote: Notify their health care provider if their weight fluctuates 2 pounds in one day or 5 pounds in one week.

sections.nursing_care.3.quote: The patient’s response to diuretic therapy is monitored by daily weights, adhering to strict intake and output.

sections.patient_teaching.0.quote: The classic presentation of HF includes lower extremity edema, weight gain, cough, sputum production, and alterations in hemodynamics.

sections.patient_teaching.1.quote: A sodium-restricted diet (less than 2000 mg of sodium per day) may help maintain euvolemia (normal blood volume) and prevent clients from becoming overloaded with fluid (which presents as pitting edema in the extremities, abdominal edema, and/or pulmonary edema).

sections.patient_teaching.2.quote: Take heart failure medications as prescribed by their health care provider.

sections.patient_teaching.3.quote: Monitor their weight daily or as directed by the health care provider and keep a record.

sections.patient_teaching.4.quote: Clients with heart failure often experience shortness of breath and fatigue with exercise; however, they should be encouraged to exercise as much as they are able.
